Abstract
With the growing complexity of AI models, and as well as the requirement for transparency and trust, integrating XAI 
into IoT applications is gaining greater momentum. Most traditional AI models are regarded as "black boxes," in which 
understanding decision-making processes presents a challenge in crucial domains such as healthcare, smart cities, and 
industrial automation. This paper looks at various methodologies of XAI that can be used to increase interpretability 
and offer better insight into the AI models of IoT environments. This research follows a taxonomy-based approach in 
the classification of ante-hoc and post-hoc XAI techniques, with the main focus on model-agnostic methods such as 
tree Explainer SHAP and LIME. Various real-world use cases are analysed for the effectiveness of XAI in enhancing trust, 
reducing biases, and improving the accuracy of decision-making in IoT systems. Challenges associated with the trade-off 
between model complexity and interpretability while maintaining efficiency are discussed. The results indicated that XAI 
techniques could significantly enhance the transparency and trust of IoT applications on account of clear and interpret-
able explanations of AI-driven decisions. These findings have been considered most effective in domains where ethical 
compliance and accountability are considered paramount. The study also points to the contribution of XAI in optimizing 
energy efficiency and improving data security in IoT frameworks. The integration of XAI into IoT systems bridges the 
gap in transparency and opens ways for scalable, trustworthy, and ethical AI applications. Of course, scalability chal-
lenges have to be overcome, and further security mechanisms have to be developed in future research to realize the 
full potential of XAI in IoT domains.
Article Highlights
•	 XAI methods have, to a great extent, helped trust, explain, and give transparency with accountability in IoT systems, 
showing in detail and vividly how the AI-driven decisions were arrived at.

1  Introduction
Artificial intelligence (AI) has, for a long time, been mostly a theoretical discipline with few practical applications. Machine 
Learning (ML) has advanced and seen broad industry acceptance over the last decade because of many factors, including 
more powerful computers, better learning algorithms, and easier access to massive quantities of data. It has caused a 
dramatic shift in this area [1]. Consequently, many practical issues in many fields, ranging from healthcare and retail to 
finance and medicine, are now being addressed via machine learning models [2]. Machine learning models have been 
on the rise in recent years, with impressive results in fields as diverse as image identification, recommendation systems, 
and natural language processing [3]. However, as these models become more sophisticated and robust, they tend to 
function like black boxes, making it hard for people to understand how they make decisions. This lack of Interpretability 
increases concerns about trust, justice, and responsibility in automated systems [4].
A new area of study called Explainable AI (XAI) has arisen in response to these problems; its practitioners work to 
improve methods and tools that make the logic of machine learning models more transparent to humans [5]. Explainable 
AI aims to provide explanations that anybody can comprehend, even when sophisticated models have a high predictive 
potential. While precision is vital in machine learning, knowing why and how a model concludes is just as critical [6]. It 
is of the utmost importance in fields like healthcare, banking, and autonomous systems, where choices affect people’s 
lives. In addition to improving transparency, XAI aids in identifying any biases, prejudice, and mistakes in the decision-
making process by offering interpretable reasons for model results [7].
Although extensive research has been conducted on XAI techniques, their application in IoT remains underexplored. 
Current studies often focus on isolated use cases, failing to provide a comprehensive framework that integrates XAI 
methodologies with the practical requirements of IoT systems. Additionally, there is limited exploration of how XAI can 
address challenges such as balancing model complexity with interpretability, ensuring data security, and achieving 
energy efficiency in resource-constrained IoT environments. This paper bridges this gap by systematically analysing XAI 
techniques, proposing a taxonomy of methods, and evaluating their applicability in diverse IoT contexts.
In machine learning, Interpretability refers to a multi-dimensional term. It requires knowing which characteristics 
or input variables are most important for a model to make a judgment [8]. It is also part of understanding the model’s 
underlying workings, including its learnt representations, weights, and decision rules. In addition to including static 
explanations, Interpretability also considers dynamic characteristics, such as how the model reacts to changes in input 
features and how well it withstands adversarial assaults [9]. However, obstacles exist on the road to Interpretability in 
ML models. As more complicated models often forego transparency in favour of enhanced performance, a fundamental 
trade-off exists between model complexity and Interpretability [10]. Finding the better spot between the two demands 
creative approaches that can streamline intricate models without sacrificing precision. Another difficulty, particularly in 
applications dealing with sensitive data, is protecting privacy and private information [11].
People often refer to profound learning AI models as “black boxes.” Such frameworks don’t always provide noticeable 
results, even when they do. Fintech AI might one day turn down loan applications or help doctors find rare illnesses [12]. 
No matter the accuracy of these facts, the developers cannot fathom them. The danger that concealed biases or mistakes 
may have real-world consequences would increase if users distrusted any system that lacked openness [13]. The deci-
sions and outcomes of an interpretable model may give developers greater confidence. This article lays the framework 
for understanding the inner workings of an AI system [14].

New explanation styles for measuring AI systems’ interpretability and transparency have led to interpretable and trans-
parent ML models, which have enormous potential for IoT settings and new approaches to explain black box decision 
systems. IoT systems may use technological explanatory strategies to ensure ethical XAI models [15]. An IoT XAI system 
has been proven to improve transparency by providing model-independent explanations. However, high-risk Internet 
of Things applications must overcome the challenge of random fresh samples. Learning domain-specific properties 
using LIME-based XAI models ensures accurate information handling and explanations. Data-driven optimization of XAI 
models may avoid model modifications for non-linear data, a major issue [12, 16]. XAI systems require new models that 
can handle theoretical and real-world explanation and interpretability, even if completely interpretable models are still 
developing. For instance, AI models’ decision-making processes may not be safe enough to protect user information and 
security in IoT devices. IoT applications must be explained, especially in healthcare and defence, which might benefit 
from XAI. Internet of Things (IoT) and associated technologies may soon use XAI [16, 17].
One very interesting example of XAI incorporation in IoT is the health sector. Explainable models, like SHAP, interpret 
patient data gathered through different wearable devices and enable health professionals to understand what factors 
determine risk predictions for chronic diseases before making proper decisions on their treatment [22]. In turn, XAI tech-
niques in smart cities have improved anomaly detection in IoT-enabled traffic management by providing interpretable 
insights that help reduce congestion and improve public safety through the mediation of abnormal traffic patterns. 
These examples illustrate how XAI can effectively translate theoretical advances into tangible benefits, building trust 
and operational efficiency in these critical IoT domains.
Despite the growing interest in Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), current methods often fall short when applied 
to real-world IoT scenarios. Traditional black-box models, while powerful, lack transparency, making it difficult for stake-
holders to trust or validate their decisions [20]. Moreover, existing XAI frameworks are frequently model-specific, limit-
ing their adaptability across diverse IoT domains such as healthcare, smart cities, and industrial automation [21]. These 
limitations underscore the urgent need for robust, scalable XAI solutions capable of addressing the unique challenges 
posed by IoT systems, including high data heterogeneity, security concerns, and real-time decision-making requirements.
The primary aim of this work is to:
1.	 A taxonomy based on ante-hoc and post-hoc approaches that give clear advice regarding the systematic analysis of 
the global XAI methodologies.
2.	 Assess the impact of interpretable and explainable AI models on decisions, indicating how they foster trust and 
openness to demonstrate their efficacy in domain-specific IoT applications.
3.	 Enhancing AI model interpretability while maintaining efficiency by incorporating innovative tactics with model-
agnostic methodologies.
4.	 Establishing transparent understandability to enhance and evaluate the trustworthiness of Interpretability and 
explainability in IoT-based applications.
The remaining sections of the document are organized as follows: The work’s literature review is detailed in Sect. 2. 
The idea behind the suggested model is discussed in Sect. 3. The performance assessment of the proposed model is 
discussed in Sect. 4. Section 5 provides suggestions for further study and serves as the paper’s last section.
2  Related survey
Using Explainable AI (XAI) approaches, the article [18] presents (XAI-IoB) that explores the Internet of Behavior (IoB) and 
how it may be used to change the behaviour of Internet of Things (IoT) devices in order to influence user behaviour. 
The goal is to deliver a trustworthy and apparent experience. Hence, we present an IoB and XAI-based system with the 
goal of influencing user behaviour and demonstrating its efficacy in a power consumption use case. Our trials show that 
power usage and cost are both reduced. Using the initial historical average consumption over 200 h, the scenario results 
demonstrated a 522.2 kW reduction in active power.
The study [19] offers a fresh and comprehensive framework for tackling IoT problems using explainable AI (XAI), deep 
learning, and progressive computing (XAI-DL). Gamian angular field converts sensor IoT data into an image database. 
Images are learned using VGG16, which uses XAI and hyper-parameter tuning. Analysis of input values’ effects on out-
put and comprehending the weights of a deep learning model employed in the learning process help us analyses IoT

In order to detect distributed denial of service (DDoS) assaults, the article [24] suggests a new approach (XAI-DDoS)

for each anomalous case and assigns a threshold to each feature. The comparative findings reveal that compared to the 
state-of-the-art methodologies, the suggested method offers better detection accuracy and attack certainty.
In [25], researchers provide a novel framework powered by XAI with Deep Neural Networks (XAI-DNN) to identify IoT 
network intrusions and attacks and interpret ML/DL-based IDS decisions. The paper construct many XAI models on top 
of the DNN architecture to boost cyber security professionals’ trust, openness, and explanation of our ML/DL-based IDS’s 
judgments. The proposed method works and is understandable after extensive trials with prevalent IoT risks.
The growing importance of explainable AI in the Internet of Things (XAIoT) is highlighted in the study [23], which 
provides a thorough examination of these protocols. In order to shed light on its real-world applications, we performed 
a case study that looked at a situation where XAIoT greatly improved IoT security. When it comes to detecting anomalies 
in IoT applications, for example, our research shows that stronger security standards and the use of powerful machine-
learning algorithms are urgently needed.
The article [24] proposes explainable AI (xAI), a new subfield of AI, to help in SDM interpretation. Utilizing complex 
statistical or machine learning models, including boosted regression trees, neural networks, and random forests, xAI 
enables the generation of SDM predictions that are more understandable and clearer. The paper explains the reasoning 
behind xAI and provides ecological modellers with a list of tools to explore the multi-scale behaviour of models. Finally, 
the paper discusses these approaches’ potential benefits and drawbacks and suggests they might help make machine-
learning SDMs easier to understand.
The open literature has not investigated the possibilities of XAI in a number of domains, including manufacturing, 
security, healthcare, and IoT networks. Additionally, it is still necessary to investigate, from the standpoint of smart homes 
to smart cities, how XAI and the Internet of Things (IoT) may be integrated comprehensively. Because of these problems, 
the article decided to look into the topic of XAI integration with IoT services in depth. In particular, the article includes 
a state-of-the-art study of XAI’s uses in many types of Internet of Things applications, including healthcare, smart cities, 
security, and industrial. Finally, for every IoT app, the paper briefly explains the most important takeaways from the poll.
3  Proposed model
As AI systems become more widespread, their correct considerations become more important. Concerns about AI’s 
fairness, transparency, and ethics should be at the bottom of our list. Creating algorithms and frameworks to guarantee 
AI systems behave ethically and transparently is a major theoretical step in AI ethics. Artificial intelligence systems may 
perpetuate social biases via algorithmic prejudice. More open and bias-free AI decision-making is the aim of fairness-
aware algorithms and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Mathematical AI frameworks and programs strive to achieve 
many goals, including processing massive volumes of data with little to no human intervention, increasing flexibility, 
and decreasing error rates. There is a lot of focus on finding ways to reduce energy use, increase computing efficiency, 
and create models that make optimal use of data. Federated learning has been buzzing recently to improve data security 
and privacy via training AI models on several distributed IoT devices. These fundamental advancements increase AI’s 
capabilities and provide the groundwork for real-world applications that might revolutionize whole sectors and improve 
people’s lives globally.
When talking about XAI, one of the biggest problems is the overuse of terms, which makes it harder to grasp what 
people are trying to say. The paper will try to provide a consistent rendition of the similarities and differences between

"white box" describes a model when all its parameters and architectural details are understood. Although this model 
type is well-suited to fostering trust, the data is sometimes insufficient to explain the reasoning behind the judgments 
thoroughly. The term "transparent box" describes a model when it provides sufficient explanation for the end-user on 
its design, parameters, or method. This openness allows one to verify, assess, and enhance the forecasts. The decision-
making process in a "black-box" model is unknown since its design and parameters are concealed. Because of their in-
depth design, DL models are often opaque, making them black box models. Next, we provide definitions of the three 
main concepts used in the XAI sector. As a result, distinguishing between these concepts is more challenging. The term 
"understandability" describes how well someone unfamiliar with the decision-making process and method can under-
stand a model’s features, functions, and characteristics.
For a model to be interpretable, one must be familiar with its inner workings and traits. The provided vocabulary 
explains the precise choice in a way that the intended customer may comprehend, making it meaningful, clear, and 
logical. Based on their application and breadth, research groups may often group explanations of AI models into one 
of three types.
While AI model choices may be justified by a few parameters in the Compact Explanation, all possible characteristics 
and facts are included in the Complete Explanation. The black box of DNN models may be concisely explained using the 
most used XAI approaches for some cases. For instance, the linear model may be presented using regression weights, 
although this technique only accounts for a small subset of neural networks. A model-specific constraint is the lack of 
generalizability to other black-box models. Model Agnostic is an alternative method that can describe all kinds of ML 
models. Although model-agnostic explanation tools are ideal due to their adaptability, they cannot access the model’s 
internal data.
Unlike the post-hoc scheme, which only shows the path to a particular result, the ante-hoc explanation scheme may 
record data from every model layer, including the input, hidden, and output layers. In contrast to the decision-tree tech-
nique, which can describe the whole model, the LIME method can only describe the steps that led to a specific ML model 
result. Post hoc procedures, like the model-agnostic approach, are more adaptable and straightforward to use with many 
models than ante-hoc strategies. The acronym XAI has been used interchangeably with a lot of different terms. Below, 
you will find an explanation and mention of some well-known terminology.

Responsible AI and Ethical AI: Both words about the XAI domain are often used. To be considered "ethical," an AI model 
must adhere to all user-defined rules and regulations when making decisions. In addition to explaining the AI model, 
deploying "responsible AI" in the real world requires privacy, justice, and ethics. When a user reasonably expects the 
model’s performance, we say the AI model is "trustworthy." On the other hand, when an AI model is safe, we say that it 
is not. Improving XAI’s credibility is vital to achieving another objective: safe AI. To reduce the possibility of accidental 
damage occurring during system-human interactions, the "Safe AI" may be able to regulate the likelihood of unforeseen 
choices.
With the rise of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), many approaches have been developed to decipher the com-
plex inner workings of machine learning models. Some recent publications have attempted to synthesize these tech-
niques and provide a basic overview of the differences between XAI methods. While several articles have addressed 
certain domains, such as healthcare or medical applications, there is a significant lack of up-to-date information about 
the current techniques and their limitations in all areas of XAI-enabled IoT applications. A thorough analysis covering 
several dimensions, including varied needs, appropriate XAI methods, and domain-specific constraints, is necessary to 
fill this need. It is essential to do this kind of study so that users may better comprehend how XAI approaches function 
in practical settings. Applying these ideas to other domains presents possibilities and limitations, which may be better 
understood using this tool. It may be accomplished by closing this gap by constructing more efficient and trustworthy 
XAI systems for IoT applications that are customized to certain domains and their distinct traits. Artificial intelligence is 
finding applications in previously unimaginable fields (Fig. 2).
➣Role of XAI deployment in IoT Systems:
XAI models have improved wireless communication services and the Internet of Things (IoT) as smart gadgets prolifer-
ate. The demand for smart IoT devices with increasing autonomy and trustworthy and transparent human relationships 
is developing. The growth of on-premises and cloud computing allows IoT devices to gather, process, and analyses 
local data. XAI models are needed to boost trust in data collecting, processing, and analysis and to perform a variety of 
autonomous tasks as AI grows. There are two primary Internet of Things use cases for XAI frameworks. First, they may be 
the brains of IoT systems, which may be used for intelligent decision-making, anomaly detection, and predictive analyt-
ics. This hub analyses IoT data using XAI models. Using XAI models to analyses and anticipate smart machine operational 
management and predictive maintenance in industries may optimize workgroup time and resources during production. 
Smart city applications may also depend on IoT devices to forecast crucial attributes. With IoT devices, vertical domain 
applications like smart cities, industries, automobiles, and grids may generate vast volumes of data. In such cases, ana-
lytics platform dependability is crucial. XAI models provide this capability and powerful smart city services by providing 
appropriate reasons for the system’s actions.

➣XAI to Strengthen Internet of Things Device Security:
It is very difficult for network managers to anticipate the complexity of current assaults on the data flow from Internet 
of Things devices across networks. The massive amounts of data generated by IoT devices can be severely disrupted if 
they are unable to identify patterns in the assaults in order to anticipate assaults on possible network assets. This XAI-
based architecture controls the flow of data pertaining to network security. In a similar vein, the authors have compiled 
a snapshot of recent developments in XAI, with a particular emphasis on malware classification, and have interpreted 
their findings via meaningful visualization. When it comes to understanding the decision-making process, DL frameworks 
based on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) might be useful for detecting cyber threats against Internet of Things (IoT) 
devices. In this case, the built modules are combined with a set of detectors, and the Internet of Things devices’ resilience 
is put to the test with Modbus network traffic.
Additionally, a detection accuracy of around 99% was found to be provided by the LSTM modules. For the purpose 
of identifying unusual communications between air traffic control and surveillance-broadcast systems a convolutional 
LSTM encoder-decoder model is used. In particular, the prediction of anomalies in the picture sequence and the expla-
nation of operational information to pilots in the process of anomaly detection for appropriate decision-making are key 
components.
It showed that XAI frameworks can make IoT device penetration and attacks observable in XAI-based security appli-
cations. XAI’s key benefit is that it shows the consequences of attacks on IoT devices, allowing for the development of 
appropriate countermeasures to guarantee the safe and secure transit of data between IoT network nodes. XAI simplifies 
stakeholder decision-making for modern communication networks to secure and manage IoT device activities supported 
by B5G/6G services. AI for Healthcare Support Systems Built on the Internet of Things: Despite the prevalent role of IoT 
devices in healthcare, the XAI concept, when integrated with healthcare data gathered from IoT devices, may improve 
the security of IoT data, increase transparency when using IoT data to forecast health information, and more.
➣XAI in IoMT applications:
The IoMT devices used to measure patients’ health metrics may play a significant role in driving the XAI models used 
for illness diagnosis and prognosis. In addition, the XAI models’ core operating processes are widely used in IoMT-based 
illness diagnosis and prediction, and they are very transparent. They are also expected to provide patients with reason-
able explanations for the model’s judgments. When it comes to the ethical and legal considerations surrounding medical 
diagnosis, the XAI model is useful as well. More importantly, the XAI model’s computation costs depend on the number 
of training samples, layers, and neurons per hidden layer. To guarantee that the AI built into IoT devices can automatically 
provide explanations, it is necessary to observe how a bigger set of people and devices interact with them. It may be 
used in healthcare services and smart homes to explain the choices made by IoT devices in a trustworthy and depend-
able way. For instance, the XAI model may alert patients’ loved ones and healthcare providers with suitable explanations 
when their depression levels are too high.
➣XAI in IoT applications:
Threats to industrial cybersecurity are growing in tandem with the use of interconnected systems in production, accord-
ing to XAI research for the IoT. Consequently, IT professionals must work together to adapt Industry 4.0 and develop 
cybersecurity measures that take use of the finest parts of the digital ecosystem in order to increase privacy and security. 
Many initiatives have been launched to ensure that IoT data used in smart manufacturing is reliable. For instance, cyber-
physical-human analysis guarantees human–machine trust, which improves cognitive prediction, human–machine inter-
action, and dynamic modelling. Industry mechatronics systems, as well as their shift to private cloud-based IoT and CPS. 
When it comes to smart industry supply chain data, Secure Blockchain Tokenizer is also used to encrypt IoT information.
➣IoT Products for Smart Cities using XAI:
International governments are rushing to incorporate artificial intelligence and other cutting-edge technology into all 
facets of their controlled urban areas. The majority of the components include e-governance, water supply, sanitation, 
public transit, electricity, and information technology connection. It is now feasible to implement smart city initiatives 
because to advancements in artificial intelligence, the internet of things, and big data. Internet of Things (IoT) devices

To summarize, the XAI’s intrinsic strengths and maturity allow it to alter IoT application domains, working in tandem 
with other supporting technologies to impart trustworthy services. In addition to improving operations and allowing 
end users to see the reasoning behind smart devices’ actions, these technologies also promise more flexible deployment 
of IoT infrastructure. However, new research issues are appearing as XAI and IoT technologies grow, and the academic 
community has to solve them. In this part, we will go over the pros, cons, and overall state of interoperability across IoT 
apps that rely on XAI.
➣Benefits of Internet of Things Systems Built on XAI:
Numerous corporate behemoths have already embraced the trend of integrating AI with IoT. But if they examine 
the decision-making process of AI systems coupled with IoT frameworks, they may get a competitive edge in real-time 
decision-making. Internet of Things (IoT) data analysis is the last but inevitable step in the process, even though IoT’s 
primary functions are to use the data stream collected from end-user sensors (e.g., smart machines and environmental 
monitoring systems) connected to the Internet. Even while AI models are vital for gleaning these patterns from IoT 
data, they don’t show consumers the decision-making process steps. By implementing XAI models, these capabilities of 
investigating system decision-making processes using data supplied by IoT devices may be unlocked.

3.1  SHAP (SHapley Additive explanations)
One well-liked method for providing context for the results produced by any machine learning model is SHAP (SHapley 
Additive explanations). It measures each coalition member’s impact using Shapley values derived from cooperative game 
theory. Determining the extent to which each feature contributes to the disparity between the predicted value and a 
baseline reference value, it then assigns credit or blame to each feature according to the amount by which it moves the 
prediction away from the baseline, thereby attributing the importance of each feature to the final prediction. The Shapley 
value may be used in the context of feature attribution within machine learning to determine the relative importance of 
each input information in predicting the model. To rephrase, a feature’s SHAP value indicates how much it contributed 
to the discrepancy between the model’s actual and expected outputs. Equation (9) provides a formal definition of the 
SHAP value of a feature for a certain instance n.
For instance n , ∅x(n) stands for the SHAP value of feature x . Remember that M is the sum of all input features, and

Relevance ranks characteristics in absolute SHAP. In addition to overall prediction, SHAP values describe each circum-
stance. Likewise, one can use it to explain forecasts and features. SHAP-based explanations may help to evaluate model

Another post-hoc ML model explanation method is Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME). Users 
may trust AI systems more after the LIME dispute. Besides being locally accurate for the model, LIME strives to provide 
understandable explanations. The "local surrogate model" is created to simplify LIME’s prediction. Examining the sim-
pler model’s feature significance values may explain this local surrogate model. They train it on perturbed instances 
around n . LIME uses interpretable models like decision trees or logistic regression to approximate the model locally. 
It then explains by perturbing the input instance and watching how it affects the model’s output. Local surrogate 
models with an interpretability requirement may be mathematically stated as Eq. (10).
For each given instance n , LIME creates an explanation model r , which minimizes a loss function P , to explain the 
model’s prediction. The loss function measures the degree to which the r-model approximates the original e-model’s 
forecast. It should be noted that F denotes the set of potential explanations (for instance, all feasible linear regression 
models) and that 휋n correlates to the neighbourhood size around the instance n that is considered for the explanation. 
To prioritize fewer features, the regularization term Ω(r) that corresponds to the complexity of the model is kept low. 
To assist consumers in understanding how different characteristics contribute to the prediction, LIME may be used to 
depict the feature significance values in various ways, such as a bar chart. Users may get insight into the logic under-
lying the model’s predictions and use it for debugging and model improvement with the LIME-based explanation.

4.1  Accuracy and transparency in decision‑making with XAI
Human and AI collaboration is crucial to fulfilling compliance and regulatory obligations. To guarantee openness and 
regulatory compliance, enterprises may use explainable AI to provide reasons and proof for AI systems’ choices (refer 
to Fig. 5a and b). An accurate and adaptable communication system is set to be developed for the next generation of 
communication between infrastructure and IoT devices. Effective communication offers the possibility of adaptively 
improving the retail market, since consumers at the edge devices with XAI capabilities may properly identify judg-
ments made based on the understanding the theoretical data in real-time. Nevertheless, a significant challenge in the 
grammatical conversation for the Internet of Things is selecting XAI models that strike a compromise between clarity in 
decision-making and transmission accuracy. There may be additional obstacles to efficient, meaningful collaboration 
due to the openness and reliability of IoT frameworks. In the long run, this collaborative learning process enhances the 
AI system’s performance. When people and AI work together, they may play to one another’s strengths, boosting the 
explainable AI market.
4.2  Efficient energy transmission and low energy consumption in IoT devices
As per Fig. 6a and b, a plethora of novel approaches to designing energy-efficient Internet of Things (IoT) devices and 
related edge devices have been put out in the last few years. On the other hand, energy drain is an inevitable conse-
quence of the pervasiveness of the Internet of Things. Further complicating matters is the fact that various situations 
and kinds of IoT frameworks may call for varied levels of comprehension and implementation of critical energy-efficient 
strategies. The combination of XAI approaches may effectively tackle the issue of large-scale network distribution, which 
has become an unavoidable trend in AI-enabled IoT solutions. One example is an Internet of Things (IoT) architecture that 
uses pre-allocated network and device resources to maximize efficiency while decreasing energy usage. To rephrase, a 
promising area of study is the development of an easily implementable, simple XAI model that may significantly improve 
the reliability of IoT systems while reducing their power consumption.

5  Conclusion
This study underlines the important role that Explainable Artificial Intelligence can play in increasing the trust, transpar-
ency, and ethical integrity of IoT applications. The study addresses the challenges in the interpretability of conventional 
AI models and shows how XAI techniques bridge the gap between model complexity and user understanding. It uses 
a taxonomy-based framework to review the efficiency of various ante-hoc and post-hoc XAI methods, including SHAP 
and LIME, in terms of transparent, actionable explanations of AI-driven decisions.
The results showed that XAI increases the accuracy and accountability of decision-making in high-stake IoT applica-
tions like healthcare, smart cities, and industrial automation. This work has emphasized how XAI will contribute to the 
reduction of bias, improvement in energy efficiency, and further improvement in security of IoT frameworks. Further, the 
integration of model-agnostic methods will be better at adapting to a wide range of IoT use cases, thus assuring wider 
applicability and scalability.
In the future, further research on some key issues is recommended, including: a hybrid XAI framework can be designed 
to combine both ante-hoc and post-hoc approaches for interpretability without compromising model performance; scal-
ability challenges need to be considered when large-scale IoT deployments integrate XAI into the real world; enhance-
ment in the robustness of XAI models against adversarial attacks will make XAI models secure and reliable in sensitive 
applications. It creates finally interdisciplinary collaboration among the research in AI, domain experts, and industry 
stakeholders who will result in practical, ethical, user-centred solutions regarding XAI.

Abstract: With the growing complexity of AI models, and as well as the requirement for transparency and trust, integrating XAI into IoT applications is gaining greater momentum. Most traditional AI models are regarded as "black boxes," in which understanding decision-making processes presents a challenge in crucial domains such as healthcare, smart cities, and industrial automation. This paper looks at various methodologies of XAI that can be used to increase interpretability and offer better insight into the AI models of IoT environments. This research follows a taxonomy-based approach in the classification of ante-hoc and post-hoc XAI techniques, with the main focus on model-agnostic methods such as tree Explainer SHAP and LIME. Various real-world use cases are analysed for the effectiveness of XAI in enhancing trust, reducing biases, and improving the accuracy of decision-making in IoT systems. Challenges associated with the trade-off between model complexity and interpretability while maintaining efficiency are discussed. The results indicated that XAI techniques could significantly enhance the transparency and trust of IoT applications on account of clear and interpret- able explanations of AI-driven decisions. These findings have been considered most effective in domains where ethical compliance and accountability are considered paramount. The study also points to the contribution of XAI in optimizing energy efficiency and improving data security in IoT frameworks. The integration of XAI into IoT systems bridges the gap in transparency and opens ways for scalable, trustworthy, and ethical AI applications. Of course, scalability chal- lenges have to be overcome, and further security mechanisms have to be developed in future research to realize the full potential of XAI in IoT domains.
